# The Turning of the Tide

## Chapter One: Low Water

The mud lay open to the sky that morning, the way it did only at the lowest tides
of the year. Mara walked out across it in her father's old boots, each step
pulling free with a soft, reluctant sound. Out here, between the sea wall and the
distant grey line of the water, the marsh held its breath. Curlews picked at the
flats, and far off a heron stood motionless, as patient as the land itself.

She had come to see the breach. For thirty years the dyke had kept the sea out of
these fields, and her grandfather had farmed them, and his father before him. Now
the engineers had cut a gap in the bank, and twice a day the salt water came back
across ground that had been dry for a lifetime.

## Chapter Two: The Flood

The tide turned while she watched. It came not as a wave but as a slow brightening
of the channels, the water creeping up the old furrows, filling the low places
first. By noon the fields she remembered as wheat were a shining sheet, and the
gulls had found it, wheeling and crying as if the sea had always been here.

Mara thought of her grandfather, who would have called this a ruin. But she
thought too of the eels that had vanished from the river, and the geese that no
longer came, and she found she could not name the feeling that rose in her. It
was not quite grief, and not quite hope.

## Chapter Three: High Water

By evening the water stood at its full height, level and silver under a pale sky.
She turned back towards the wall, her boots heavy now, and stopped once to look
behind her. The marsh had taken the field, and somewhere under the bright water
the old furrows were softening, year by year, into something the map would one day
call by another name.
